newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia voices growing concern over hostages.
newsitem.headline: Colombia voices growing concern over hostages.

text.p: Colombia's Interior Minister said on Wednesday the government was growing increasingly concerned about the fate of at least 60 soldiers taken prisoner by leftist guerrillas on Aug. 30.
"The fact that this is taking so long is of great concern to us," Horacio Serpa said of the hostage situation.

"It's been more than 15 days already," Serpa added in an interview with the Caracol radio network, noting that Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) had originally pledged to arrange the soldiers' prompt release.
The government said in a communique issued on Tuesday night that it would offer any "reasonable guarantees needed" to ensure the soldiers were released as soon as possible.

But Serpa noted in his comments to Caracol that the FARC had failed to make any specific demands, or lay down specific conditions, for the handover of the hostages to a special commission headed by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

FARC rebels seized anywhere from 60 to 67 soldiers and killed 27 others when they overran the Las Delicias military base in a remote area of the jungle-covered southern province of Putumayo on Aug. 30.

The attack, which humiliated military commanders in Bogota, came at the start of what authorities have described as the bloodiest rebel offensive Colombia has seen in more than three decades of guerrilla warfare.
In a speech on Tuesday, President Ernesto Samper said international law called for the soldiers' earliest possible release.

The hostages should not be submitted to "the humiliation of an advertising campaign," Samper said, referring to suspected FARC efforts to use their captives as a bargaining chip in a high stakes bid to win international recognition as a legitimate political force.

Government and military officials have long dismissed the FARC, Latin America's largest and oldest rebel group, as nothing more than armed bandits involved in kidnapping, extortion and drug trafficking.
